headlines.summary: Nvidia says its DSX Pod AI Factory, which combines seven Vera Rubin racks in a shipping container, could cut the time to start serving AI tokens to 14 days.
headlines.article_text: Nvidia announces Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia's new DSX Pod AI Factory packages seven Vera Rubin AI racks in a shipping container designed to be transported by truck. All the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory. Nvidia did not disclose a price; analysts estimate a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., shows Vera Rubin computer modules during the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC in Berlin, Germany, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty Images Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing. The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said. "The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week. The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers. Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027. Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated. "What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up." Carlos Barria | Reuters OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies. For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers. Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models . Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks. "Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively. All three report quarterly results next week. Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model. OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering. Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface. Musk also said that SpaceX and Tesla , his auto manufacturer, have formed special committees to discuss a merger. Tesla shares were up 1%. Space stocks — Other aerospace companies were higher following SpaceX's earnings jump. Rocket Lab rose 2.5%, while AST SpaceMobile was higher by almost 3%. Firefly Aerospace jumped 3.5%. Netflix — Shares of Netflix fell almost 7% after the streaming giant reported third-quarter revenue that was in line with Wall Street's expectations. Sales came in at $12.87 billion, up 12% year over year, boosted by growth in membership and an increase in subscription prices that went into effect in March, the company said. AT & T — The telecommunications company slid 3.5% despite reporting an earnings and revenue beat in its third-quarter financial report. AT & T also hiked its full-year earnings guidance, though it reiterated capital expenditures that came in slightly above expectations, according to FactSet. Capital One Financial — The lender and credit card issuer gained 3% in premarket trading. Third-quarter net income reached $3.5 billion, or $5.61 per share, up from $3.2 billion, or $4.83 a share a year ago. United Airlines — The Chicago-based carrier fell 1% before the bell on Wednesday. Third-quarter adjusted EPS of $2.54 on revenue of $17.88 billion trailed Wall Street consensus estimates of $2.57 per share and $17.90 billion, according to LSEG data. Super Micro Computer — Shares rallied 12% after the data center server company hiked its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook. Super Micro sees revenue for the period between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, up from a previous range of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Dell Technologies , Hewlett Packard Enterprise — Super Micro's server competitors Dell and HPE were also higher on the news of the company's guidance update. Dell was jumping by 5.5%, while HPE rose 4.5%. Revenue came in at $6.55 billion, compared to analysts polled by FactSet's expectation for $6.56 billion. Adjusted earnings, however, beat estimates, and the company raised its full-year guidance for the metric. Philip Morris International — The tobacco and consumer goods company slipped 3% after it reported better-than-expected results in its third-quarter earnings report. However, full-year 2026 earnings guidance came in below expectations, according to analysts polled by FactSet. CME Group — Shares fell 1% despite the exchange reporting better-than-expected results in its third-quarter earnings report. CME delivered adjusted earnings of $3.02 per share, compared to a FactSet forecast of $2.99 per share. Revenue also came in slightly above estimates, as did operating income. — CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Fred Imbert and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting.

headlines.title: House committee says Webull messages point to China access to U.S. customer data
headlines.summary: The House Select Committee on China earlier this month said online investing platform Webull is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government.
headlines.article_text: Webull U.S. customer data access in China questioned Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The House Select Committee on China says internal Webull messages from 2021 indicate that an employee believed to be in China had access to information about a U.S. customer account. Webull, which is an online investing platform, has said sensitive U.S. customer data is restricted to U.S.-based employees An Oct. 7 report by the select committee found that Webull is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance. In this article BULL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:46 02:46 House committee says Webull messages point to China access to U.S. customer data Squawk Box Internal messages between employees of online investing platform Webull suggest a company employee in China had access to information about a U.S. customer, despite the company having said it bars such sharing, according to an analysis of the messages by the House Select Committee on China . The analysis comes nearly two weeks after CNBC first detailed the bipartisan select committee's report that concluded that Webull, which counts 28 million users, is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance. Webull shares slid more than 19% on the heels of that Oct. 7 report. At the time of the report, Webull told CNBC in a statement that "U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S." But the newly released internal messages by the House Select Committee on China, which CNBC exclusively obtained, raise questions about whether that has always been the case. The committee has focused on threats posed by China and protecting U.S. industry from Chinese competition. One message thread suggests a Webull employee was in China during a discussion about a U.S. customer account. The thread also indicates the account was previously approved by a China Webull team member and an American counterpart. The messages, dating to 2021, were sent on Microsoft Teams between Brendan Fuller, a manager at Webull's U.S. brokerage, and an employee named Zhenghan Wang, whose nickname is "Rock." The select committee says Wang was likely in China at the time. In one message, Fuller messaged Wang about concerns involving a particular trading account. "We saw these problems ... and approve account," Fuller wrote. Wang replied: "Yes,CIP." CIP is an acronym for Customer Identification Program, a U.S. regulatory requirement that financial institutions verify the identities of individuals and entities opening accounts. "I thought so," Fuller responded. Wang asked Fuller: "Who approve the account?" Fuller responded: "One China team member and one US team." Wang then asked: "I want to know in what situation (CIP), can we approve the account open?" Fuller responded: "I think we just approve them all no matter what ..." "And then we pay for vendors. And create report and work," Fuller added. Wang then replied that "CIP=" followed by Mandarin Chinese characters forming a common phrase that translates as "Exists in name only," or "Useless." A spokesperson for the select committee, in a statement to CNBC, said, "All the evidence in these text messages points to Zhenghan Wang, a Webull employee, being located in China with access to U.S. customer data at the time he worked for the company." An analysis by the committee concluded that Wang was in China at the time of the exchange because the messages' time stamps indicated that Wang was working daytime hours in Beijing, and because he set his software to translate the messages into simplified Chinese. A Webull spokesperson did not directly respond to CNBC's questions about Wang's access to U.S. customer data in 2021 and whether that disproved the company's assertion that its U.S. data does not go to China. The Webull spokesperson said, "Protecting customer data is central to Webull's operations." "Webull's U.S. customer data is stored only in the U.S. on AWS servers in Virginia and Oregon, with access to sensitive data restricted to U.S.-based employees," the spokesperson said. "U.S. broker-dealer operations are directed exclusively by U.S.-based personnel, and no individuals based outside the U.S. have ever exercised operational or decision-making authority over Webull's U.S. broker-dealer business." The company spokesperson also criticized the select committee's release of the messages. "The Teams messages now being referenced date back to a 2021 routine FINRA matter, which was concluded," the spokesperson said. FINRA, or the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, is the self-regulatory organization for member broker-dealers. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working The messages' "recent disclosure, alongside the Select Committee's report relying on preliminary and outdated information, raises legitimate questions about the timing and circumstances surrounding their release," Webull's spokesperson said. "Webull rejects irresponsible speculation and stands on our well-documented record: Webull's data protection practices are robust, continuously enhanced, and independently verified." The select committee's Oct. 7 report argued that Webull's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. Those Chinese laws can compel firms to cooperate with the government in various ways, including mandating data transfers. The select committee on Tuesday issued a press release titled, "The Facts on Webull's Ties to China." The release said that since the committee issued its report, Webull "has ... responded with numerous false statements about its business and its interactions with the Select Committee." The committee listed five claims by Webull, followed by what the committee labeled "The Truth." One section, titled "Webull Claim: 'U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S.,'" was followed by a rebuttal that said, "The Truth: The Select Committee's report does not dispute where the data is stored. "Its finding is about who can reach the data and the systems that process it," the committee continued. "The report found that Webull affiliate Webull Technologies Limited previously used Tencent Cloud, a China-based provider, to host certain user data ... Webull has not said what data Tencent hosted or when that ended." Webull said Tuesday that it was partnering with Kalshi , the prediction market platform, to offer so-called perpetual futures to U.S. customers. The first set of perpetual futures, which do not have an expiration date, as traditional futures do, would be for cryptocurrencies, Webull said. headlines.summary: MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Unicycive Therapeutics, Inc. (“Unicycive” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: UNCY), a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing therapies for patients with kidney disease, today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted the resubmission of its New Drug Application (NDA) for oxylanthanum carbonate (OLC), the Company’s investigational oral phosphate binder for the treatment of hyperphosphatemia in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) on dialysis. The NDA was resubmitted following a Complete Response Letter (CRL) received in June 2026. The FDA has deemed the OLC resubmission a Class II with a six-month review period from the resubmission date, and set a Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) target action date of March 25, 2027.
